title: The patriarchs’ troubles and Jacob’s marked flocks
source_text: Ἀτοπωτάτην δὲ λέγει καὶ ἔξωρον παιδοποιΐαν, εἰ καὶ μὴ ὠνόμασε, δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι λέγων τὴν τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τῆς Σάῤῥας. ῥίπτων δὲ καὶ τὰς τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἐπιβουλὰς ἤτοι τὸν Κάϊν ἐπιβουλεύσαντα τῷ Ἄβελ λέγει ἢ πρὸς τούτῳ καὶ τὸν Ἠσαῦ τῷ Ἰακώβ· πατρὸς δὲ λύπην, τάχα μὲν καὶ τὴν Ἰσαὰκ ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ ἀποδημίᾳ τάχα δὲ καὶ τὴν τοῦ Ἰακὼβ διὰ τὸν Ἰωσὴφ πραθέντα εἰς Αἴγυπτον. μητέρων δ᾿ οἶμαι ἐνέδρας ἀναγράφοντα αὐτὸν δηλοῦν τὴν Ῥεβέκκαν, οἰκονομήσασαν τὰς τοῦ Ἰσαὰκ εὐχὰς μὴ ἐπὶ τὸν Ἠσαῦ ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰακὼβ φθάσαι. ἄγχιστα δὲ τούτοις πᾶσι συμπολιτευόμενον εἴ φαμεν τὸν θεὸν, τί ἄτοπον πράσσομεν πειθόμενοι μηδέ ποτε ἀφιστάνειν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ θειότητα τῶν μετὰ τοῦ καλῶς καὶ ἐῤῥωμένως βιοῦν αὐτῷ ἀνακειμένων; ἐχλεύασε δὲ τὴν παρὰ τῷ Λάβαν κτῆσιν τοῦ Ἰακὼβ, μὴ νοήσας, ἐπὶ τί ἀναφέρεται τὸ „καὶ ἦν τὰ ἄσημα τοῦ Λάβαν, τὰ δὲ ἐπίσημα τοῦ Ἰακὼβ.“ καί φησι τὸν θεὸν τοῖς υἱοῖς ὀνάρια καὶ προβάτια καὶ καμήλους δεδωρῆσθαι· καὶ οὐχ ἑώρα ὅτι „ταῦτα πάντα τυπικῶς συνέβαινεν ἐκείνοις, ἐγράφη δὲ δι᾿ ἡμᾶς. εἰς οὓς τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντησε“· παρ᾿ οἷς τὸ ποικίλα ἤθη „ἐπίσημα“ γινόμενα τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ πολιτεύεται, δοθέντα κτῆσις τῷ τροπικῶς καλουμένῳ Ἰακώβ. ἀπὸ γὰρ τῶν ἐθνῶν οἱ εἰς αὐτὸν πιστεύοντες ἐδηλοῦντο διὰ τῶν ἀναγεγραμμένων περὶ Λάβαν καὶ Ἰακώβ.
pass_a_gloss: He calls (it) a most absurd (ἀτοπωτάτην) and untimely/past-season (ἔξωρον) child-begetting (παιδοποιΐαν), even if he did not name it, but clearly meaning that of Abraham and Sarah. And throwing in (ῥίπτων) also the plots (ἐπιβουλάς) of brothers, he means either Cain having plotted against Abel or, in addition to this, also Esau against Jacob; and a father's grief (λύπην), perhaps that of Isaac at the departure (ἀποδημίᾳ) of Jacob, perhaps also that of Jacob on account of Joseph sold (πραθέντα) into Egypt. And I think that in recording mothers' ambushes/treacheries (ἐνέδρας) he indicates Rebecca, who arranged (οἰκονομήσασαν) that Isaac's prayers (εὐχάς) should reach first (φθάσαι) not upon Esau but upon Jacob. If we say God most nearly (ἄγχιστα) shares-citizenship/lives along with (συμπολιτευόμενον) all these, what absurd thing do we do, being persuaded that he never removes (ἀφιστάνειν) his own divinity (θειότητα) from those devoted (ἀνακειμένων) to him with living nobly and strongly (ἐρρωμένως)? He jeered at (ἐχλεύασε) the acquisition (κτῆσιν) of Jacob at Laban's, not understanding to what is referred (ἀναφέρεται) the 'and the unmarked (ἄσημα) were Laban's, and the marked (ἐπίσημα) Jacob's'. And he says God has given (δεδωρῆσθαι) to the sons little asses (ὀνάρια) and little sheep (προβάτια) and camels; and he did not see that 'all these things happened to them typically (τυπικῶς), and were written for our sake (δι' ἡμᾶς), unto whom the ends (τέλη) of the ages (αἰώνων) have arrived (κατήντησε)'; among whom the varied/spotted characters (ποικίλα ἤθη), becoming 'marked' by the word (λόγῳ) of God, live as citizens (πολιτεύεται), given as possession (κτῆσις) to the one figuratively (τροπικῶς) called Jacob. For those from the nations (ἐθνῶν) believing in him were signified (ἐδηλοῦντο) through the things recorded about Laban and Jacob.
pass_b_english: He speaks of “a most absurd and untimely begetting of children”; although he has not named it, he clearly means that of Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 18:11–14; Genesis 21:1–2). And when he tosses in “the plots of brothers,” he means either Cain plotting against Abel (Genesis 4:8) or, besides him, Esau against Jacob as well (Genesis 27:41); and by “a father’s grief” perhaps Isaac’s at Jacob’s going away, and perhaps also Jacob’s over Joseph, who was sold into Egypt (Genesis 37:28; Genesis 37:34–35). And in writing of “the treacheries of mothers,” I think he means Rebekah, who contrived that Isaac’s prayers should reach Jacob first, and not Esau (Genesis 27:5–29).

If we say that God shared most closely in the life of all these, what absurdity do we commit, since we are convinced that he never withdraws his own divinity from those who have devoted themselves to him and live nobly and with vigour?

He has mocked the wealth Jacob gained while with Laban, not understanding what the words refer to: “And the unmarked were Laban’s, and the marked were Jacob’s” (Genesis 30:42). And he says that God “gave his sons little donkeys and little sheep and camels”; and he did not see that “all these things happened to them as figures, and were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Among us, characters of many colours, made “marked” by the word of God, live as citizens, given as a possession to him who is figuratively called Jacob. For those from the nations who believe in him were signified by what is written about Laban and Jacob.

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 43 (Koetschau 4.43). The quoted phrases (‘a most absurd and untimely begetting of children’, ‘the plots of brothers’, ‘a father’s grief’, ‘the treacheries of mothers’, and God ‘gave his sons little donkeys and little sheep and camels’) are Celsus’s catalogue items as Origen reports them in the accusative/indirect construction; the exact limits of Celsus’s wording are not marked in this staged text. τοῖς υἱοῖς is rendered ‘his sons’ (the article as possessive); the Greek does not say whose sons. Celsus’s list of animals may echo Genesis 30:43 (sheep, camels, asses), but that is Celsus’s wording, so it is not cited inline. Isaac’s grief at Jacob’s going away is Origen’s guess (‘perhaps’) and has no explicit verse (Jacob is sent away in Genesis 28:1–5), so no citation there. εὐχαί (‘prayers’) are Isaac’s blessings; φθάσαι is ‘reach first’. Genesis 30:42 LXX: ‘ἐγένετο δὲ τὰ ἄσημα τοῦ Λαβαν, τὰ δὲ ἐπίσημα τοῦ Ιακωβ’; Origen has ἦν. 1 Corinthians 10:11: Origen reads ταῦτα πάντα τυπικῶς and ἐγράφη δὲ δι᾿ ἡμᾶς (the common text has πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν, ‘for our instruction’; ‘for our sake’ recalls 1 Corinthians 9:10); translated as he quotes it. ποικίλα ἤθη keeps the play on the speckled (ποικίλα) flocks of Genesis 30, hence ‘characters of many colours’. The construction παρ᾿ οἷς τὸ ποικίλα ἤθη … πολιτεύεται is awkward (article τό with a finite verb) and may be corrupt; rendered by sense, with πολιτεύεται as ‘live as citizens’. ‘The word of God’ is left lower case: it may be the divine Word or the message. The figurative Jacob is Christ (‘those … who believe in him’).
